sentences.text: The name Diluvicursor translates to "flood runner," a title chosen because the fossil was unearthed in a high-energy river setting.
The specific epithet pickeringi commemorates David A. Pickering, a distinguished Australian paleontologist who passed away before the research was finalized.
The primary specimen, known as the holotype, preserves an almost complete articulated tail that is missing only the first, second, and twelfth vertebrae.
Scientists identified ten unique derived traits in this animal, such as spinous processes on the third through sixth tail vertebrae that are low and no taller than their front-to-back width.
This dinosaur is notably larger than the more recent ornithischians discovered at Dinosaur Cove.
The holotype individual, classified as a juvenile subadult, measured approximately 1.2 meters in length.
Adults of this species are estimated to have reached at least 2.3 meters, a size comparable to that of an emu.
Remains of Diluvicursor were found in 2005 within the Eumeralla Formation and were formally named in early 2018 after being reported in scientific literature in 2009 by Thomas Rich and colleagues.
A partial tail vertebra belonging to a larger individual discovered nearby in the same deposit was also assigned to this taxon.
Diluvicursor was likely a plant-eater that consumed low vegetation including Pteridophyta, Hepaticae, Lycopsida, Cycadophyta, Bennettitales, and Taeniopteridae.
Researchers hypothesize that the carcass was dragged by a current and quickly deposited in a thick layer of mud, where it became entangled in tree trunks on a tree stump in a deep, high-energy river.

A low tail base indicates a special form of movement for Diluvicursor, and researchers suggest that the widening of muscles likely improved walking ability by allowing the femur to be pushed back with greater force.
Cladistic analysis places Diluvicursor within Cerapoda, and the animal belongs to the class Ornithischia.
The parent group of Diluvicursor is Elasmaria, and phylogenetic analysis recovered it as a basal elasmarian and the sister taxon to Anabisetia.

Descriptives considered the placement of Diluvicursor among Euornithopoda to be tentative, while traditional comparative methods suggest it is related to Anabisetia, Gasparinisaura, the family Dryosauridae, and possibly the Antarctic dinosaur Morrosaurus.

Diluvicursor pickeringi lived approximately 113 million years ago during the Albian stage of the Early Cretaceous in what is now Australia, specifically in Victoria, southeastern Australia, near Cape Otway during the early Albian stage between 113.2 and 110.1 million years ago.

It is debated whether Diluvicursor is synonymous with other small-bodied ornithopods from the same formation due to a lack of overlapping anatomical material, and it is also debated whether Diluvicursor is identical to Atlascopcosaurus, though evidence suggests at least two ornithischians were present at the site.
